lead: This unit is about running testing as a managed, automated activity and then shipping the result. You will write a test plan, organise and report a test team, choose what to automate, and compute test metrics. Then you will follow a commit through version control, continuous integration, a build pipeline and an Ansible deployment.
about: This unit moves from planning testing to running it as an engineering operation. Chapter 5.1 writes the test plan and its components; 5.2 staffs a test group and reports results; 5.3 decides what to automate and with which tools; 5.4 turns the resulting data into metrics for decisions. The second half follows a commit through the delivery system: 5.5 records every change in version control, 5.6 turns each change into an integrated, releasable build, 5.7 designs the build and test pipeline that produces a versioned artifact, and 5.8 configures servers with repeatable Ansible playbooks. Every chapter uses small numbers so the reasoning can be checked by hand in the exam.

chapters.idea: A test plan is the written agreement on what will be tested, how, by whom, and the rules for stopping.
chapters.depth: Why a plan exists: it is the agreed baseline for scope, effort, schedule and stopping rules. Cover plan levels: a master test plan plus level plans for unit, integration, system and acceptance testing. List the usual components in order: plan identifier and scope; test items; features to be tested; features deliberately not tested; test approach and levels; entry criteria; exit criteria; suspension and resumption rules; environment, tools and test data; deliverables; roles and responsibilities; schedule; risks and contingencies; approvals. Attachments: requirement-to-test traceability matrix, test case list, defect workflow. Locating test items means mapping each item to its test cases and back to the requirement.

figure.title: Test plan sections
figure.aria: A top-to-bottom flow of the sections of a test plan, ending with the attachments that carry the traceability matrix.

chapters.example: Question: a UPI payment feature has 45 functional requirements; plan three regression cycles inside an 18-day window with two testers. Average 3 test cases per requirement gives 135 test cases. 30% are automated, so 40 are automated and 95 stay manual. A tester runs 6 manual cases per day, so one full cycle needs 95/6 ≈ 16 person-days. Three cycles are 48 person-days, which with two testers needs 24 days and misses the window. Replace cycle 3 with a 25-case smoke subset: 16 + 16 + 25/6 ≈ 4, that is 36 person-days, which two testers finish in 18 days. The plan records entry criteria (feature complete, CI build green), exit criteria (no open severity 1 or 2 defects, 100% requirement traceability), and the risk that cycle 3 no longer covers the full regression set.
chapters.trap: Writing the plan once and never revising it, and confusing the plan with the test case specification; the most-forgotten sections are features not tested and exit criteria.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 requirements and the SRS; Unit 4 test case design
chapters.leave: Test design techniques to Unit 4; effort estimation, scheduling and risk detail to Unit 6

chapters.idea: Testing is done by people inside an organisation, so a plan works only if the team is staffed, structured and reported on properly.
chapters.depth: The people side: tester motivation, independence of testers, the natural friction between testers and developers, and the career path of a test specialist. Organisation structures: a central independent test group, testers embedded in development teams, a hybrid, and outsourced or offshore testing services; strengths and weaknesses of each. Roles: test manager, test lead, test engineer, automation engineer, performance tester, domain expert. Skills of a test specialist: domain knowledge, test design, SQL and scripting, tool use, clear defect writing, curiosity, diplomacy. Building a testing group and its structure with a span of control. A technical training program: onboarding, domain training, tool training, mentoring, certification. The test process as plan, design, execute, evaluate exit criteria, report, closure. Reporting: daily status, weekly report, test summary report, and the fields of a defect report.

figure.aria: A testing group as a hierarchy: one test manager over a functional lead with eight test engineers and an automation lead with two automation engineers.

chapters.example: Question: write the test summary for release 2.3. Of 480 executed cases, 456 passed, 24 failed and 6 were blocked, so pass rate = 456/480 = 95% and blocked rate = 6/480 = 1.25%. The 24 failures plus 6 exploratory findings gave 30 defects: 12 of severity 1 or 2, 14 of severity 3, 4 of severity 4. Of these, 27 are closed and 3 deferred. Two defects escaped to production, so leakage = 2/(30+2) = 6.25%. The group is 1 test manager, 2 leads, 8 test engineers and 2 automation engineers, a span of control of 1:6. Recommendation: release with the 3 deferred defects accepted by the product owner and fixes scheduled in 2.4.
chapters.trap: Assuming an independent test team guarantees quality, and measuring testers by the number of defects they log, which rewards testers for finding trivial defects.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 test plan, which fixes roles, schedule and exit criteria
chapters.leave: Motivation theory to management courses; effort estimation and project scheduling to Unit 6

chapters.idea: Automate the tests that are run often and change rarely, and decide with a cost calculation rather than enthusiasm.
chapters.depth: What to automate: stable, repeatable, high-volume, data-driven and regression tests, smoke suites, API and performance tests. What not to automate: new and rapidly changing features, exploratory testing, usability testing, one-off checks. Design styles: linear scripts, modular scripts, data-driven, keyword-driven, hybrid, page object model for web, behaviour-driven tests. The test pyramid: many unit tests, fewer API tests, few UI tests, and why UI-heavy suites are slow and fragile. Tool selection criteria: language and platform support, licence cost, CI integration, reporting, community, team skill. Tools to name: Selenium and Playwright for web, JUnit, TestNG and PyTest for unit level, Appium for mobile, JMeter for load, Postman for API, Cucumber for behaviour-driven tests. Return on investment from build cost, run cost and maintenance. Keep test code in version control and review it like product code.

figure.aria: Two cost lines over repeated regression runs: automation starts high and rises slowly, manual testing starts at zero and rises steeply, crossing near fifteen runs.

chapters.example: Question: should a 120-case regression suite be automated? Manual cost is 6 person-hours per run. Automation needs 60 person-hours to build, then 2 person-hours per run for maintenance. Manual over 12 runs a year costs 72 person-hours. In year 1 automation costs 60 + 24 = 84 person-hours, so it loses. Break-even is 60/(6 − 2) = 15 runs, about 15 months at this rate. Over 3 years: manual 216 person-hours against automated 60 + 72 = 132 person-hours, a saving of 84 person-hours. Decision: automate, because the suite will also grow and the product will be maintained for years.
chapters.trap: Believing automation replaces manual testing and finds new defects; automated tests only check what was already known. Ignoring maintenance cost is the second error.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 test types and test case design; 5.1 plan decides the automation scope
chapters.leave: Test design techniques to Unit 4; running the suite inside a pipeline to 5.6 and 5.7

chapters.idea: A metric turns test and defect data into a number that supports a decision, and a metric used as a target stops being a good measure.
chapters.depth: Measurement basics: base measures (counts taken directly) and derived metrics (computed from them); leading and lagging indicators; process and product metrics; Goal-Question-Metric, where you start from a goal, ask the questions that show whether it is met, then pick the metric. Metrics to cover with formulas: test execution progress, pass/fail/blocked counts, requirement, statement and branch coverage, defect density (per KLOC, per requirement, per test case), defect removal efficiency, defect leakage, severity distribution, defect arrival and closure trend, mean time between failures, availability, automation coverage, test cycle time, effort and schedule variance. Present trends, not single numbers. Pitfalls: targets that distort behaviour, and comparing metrics across dissimilar projects.

figure.aria: Cumulative defect arrival over sixteen weeks compared with cumulative closure; the gap between the two curves is the open defect backlog.

chapters.example: Question: compute four metrics for a release. Size is 15 KLOC; 90 defects were found in testing and 10 in the first six months after release; the system ran 5000 hours across installations with 8 failures; 1140 of 1200 planned test cases were executed. Defect density = 90/15 = 6 defects per KLOC. Defect removal efficiency = 90/(90+10) = 90%. Defect leakage = 10/(90+10) = 10%. MTBF = 5000/8 = 625 hours. Test execution progress = 1140/1200 = 95%. Read together: density is within the usual range, but leakage of 10% says the exit criteria were too loose.
chapters.trap: Reporting a metric as a target (for example demanding a defect density figure) and assuming high defect counts mean a bad team; a team that logs many early defects often delivers a cleaner release.
chapters.leave: Process and project metric definitions to Unit 6; statistical reliability models beyond a mention

chapters.idea: A version control system records every change as an immutable snapshot, so any past state of the project can be rebuilt exactly.
chapters.depth: Purpose: history, undo, collaboration, parallel work on branches, baselines for releases, audit trail. Vocabulary: repository, working copy, commit, revision, branch, tag, mainline or trunk, merge, conflict, baseline. Centralised systems, where one server holds all history, against distributed systems, where every clone holds full history. Git internals at working level: a commit is a snapshot of the whole tree plus a pointer to its parent, named by a hash; blobs hold file contents and trees hold directories; the commit graph is a directed acyclic graph. Commands: clone, add, commit, status, log, diff, branch, switch, merge, rebase, tag, push, pull, fetch, revert, reset, stash, and the .gitignore file. Hooks that run before commit or before push. Branching strategies: trunk-based, feature branch, release branch. Small commits and clear messages. A push or a tag is what wakes the CI server.

figure.aria: A commit graph where a feature branch splits from the mainline, gains one commit, and merges back into a merge commit that has two parents.

chapters.example: Question: merge branch feature/pay into main and predict the conflicts. The base commit of app.py has 20 lines. feature/pay inserts 6 lines after line 10 and also changes line 4. main changes line 15 and also changes line 4. Git compares both branch tips with the base: the insertion after line 10 and the change at line 15 touch different regions, so they merge automatically; line 4 changed in both, so Git stops and writes conflict markers in that region. The developer edits it, runs git add app.py, then git commit, which creates merge commit M with two parents C and E.
chapters.trap: Thinking a commit stores per-file differences, when it stores snapshots; and mixing up merge with rebase, or pull with fetch. Committing build output or passwords into the repository is the third classic error.
chapters.prereq: Unit 6 software configuration management, which defines baselines and change control
chapters.leave: Configuration management process and audits to Unit 6; the pipeline that reacts to a push to 5.6 and 5.7

chapters.idea: Continuous integration merges everyone's work into the mainline many times a day and proves each merge with an automated build and test, and continuous delivery keeps the result always deployable.
chapters.depth: Definitions to separate carefully: continuous integration means merging to the mainline at least daily, with every merge checked by an automated build and test; continuous delivery means every change is releasable, and releasing is a business decision; continuous deployment means every passing change reaches production automatically. The deployment pipeline and its stages: commit, build, unit tests, package, deploy to staging, acceptance tests, deploy to production. Practices: trunk-based development, build once and promote the same artifact, environment parity, database migrations, blue-green and canary releases, feature flags, rollback, pipeline as code. DevOps as the culture and tooling that removes the wall between development and operations; cloud as the platform on which the pipeline runs. Tools to name: Jenkins, GitLab CI, GitHub Actions, Argo CD. Some syllabi add cloud operations, deployment pipeline architecture and a case study; treat the stage order and the fail-fast rule as the exam core.

figure.aria: A twenty-six minute pipeline where integration testing is split into four parallel shards of five minutes each, followed by packaging, staging deployment and smoke tests.

chapters.example: Question: shorten a 41-minute pipeline. Stages run in series: build 5 min, unit tests 8 min, integration tests 20 min, package 3 min, deploy to staging 2 min, smoke tests 3 min, total 41 min. Split integration tests into 4 parallel shards of 5 min: that stage drops from 20 to 5 min, so the pipeline becomes 5+8+5+3+2+3 = 26 min. Splitting the 8-minute unit stage into 2 shards saves a further 4 min, giving 22 min. Deleting the smoke stage would save 3 min but removes the release gate, so it is refused.
chapters.trap: Saying a team does continuous integration because it has a Jenkins server, while branches live for weeks; and treating continuous delivery and continuous deployment as the same thing.
chapters.prereq: 5.5 version control, because a push is the trigger; 5.3 test automation supplies the tests
chapters.leave: Detailed build steps to 5.7; server configuration and deployment playbooks to 5.8; risk management to Unit 6

chapters.idea: A build and test pipeline turns a commit into a tested, versioned artifact in stages that fail fast.
chapters.depth: What a build does, in order: fetch source, resolve dependencies from a cache or artifact repository, compile, run unit tests and static analysis, package, publish the artifact. Build tools to name: Maven, Gradle, Ant, npm, MSBuild. Stage design: fail fast with the shortest tests first, parallel shards, smoke suite on every commit and full suite nightly, flaky tests moved to a quarantine lane instead of being deleted. Agents and runners, self-hosted against cloud. Artifact versioning and immutability: a name like 2.3.0-231 carries the release version and the build number; build once and promote the same artifact from dev to staging to production. Secrets kept out of the repository. Caches that cut build time. Pipeline metrics: duration, failure rate, mean time to repair, lead time for changes. Every artifact is traceable to one commit hash.

figure.title: One pipeline run
figure.aria: The stages of a build pipeline from commit to deployed development environment, ending in one immutable published artifact.

chapters.example: Question: a repository of 40 modules takes 30 minutes for a full CI build. A commit touches 3 modules. The incremental build recompiles them at 45 s each = 135 s, plus 60 s to link and package = 3 min 15 s, about one-ninth of the full build. The pipeline therefore runs the incremental build with unit tests for the touched modules on every commit, and a full build with the whole test suite once a night. The artifact is tagged 2.3.0-231, published once to the artifact repository, and promoted to staging and production without rebuilding, so all environments run byte-identical files.
chapters.trap: Rebuilding the artifact separately for each environment, so staging and production differ; and letting tests depend on execution order or on data left by an earlier run.
chapters.prereq: 5.6 pipeline stages; 5.5 commits and tags that trigger the build
chapters.leave: Test case design to Unit 4; server configuration and release to 5.8; dependency licence audits to a legal chapter

chapters.idea: Configuration management brings every server to a declared state, and a playbook does it the same way however many times you run it.
chapters.depth: Configuration management means keeping every environment in a known, declared state, written down as code. Declarative against imperative style: you describe the end state, not the steps, and the same file may be applied any number of times. The central property is idempotency: run the playbook once or ten times and the machine ends in the same state. Ansible at working level: agentless over SSH, a control node, an inventory of managed hosts grouped by role, modules, tasks, plays, playbooks written in YAML, variables and gathered facts, Jinja2 templates, handlers that run only when notified, roles for reuse, tags for partial runs, vault for secrets, and check mode for a dry run. A typical playbook installs packages, writes configuration from a template, starts and enables services, and reloads only on change. In the pipeline it provisions test environments, deploys the artifact and configures released servers. Only a few universities name a specific tool; the rest teach the same idea tool-agnostic.

figure.title: Playbook run
figure.aria: A playbook running against twelve hosts: install, template, start service, a reload handler on change, and a second run that reports no changes.

chapters.example: Question: configure 12 web servers with one playbook and show that it is idempotent. web.yml targets the inventory group web with 12 hosts, installs nginx, writes nginx.conf from a template with worker_processes = 2 × vCPU, and ensures the service is started and enabled; a handler reloads nginx only when the template output changes. First run: 3 changes per host, 36 changes, 12 hosts ok. Second run with unchanged files: 0 changes on all 12 hosts. If host 9 is unreachable, the recap shows 11 ok and 1 failed; after the network is fixed, a rerun applies tasks to host 9 only, because the other 11 already match the declared state.
chapters.trap: Writing YAML that wraps a shell script which appends a line or restarts the service every time, so the play is not idempotent; and managing secrets in plain files instead of a vault.
chapters.prereq: 5.6 deployment stage and environments; 5.7 artifacts that get deployed
chapters.leave: Container orchestration and cloud infrastructure design to a cloud elective; general operations procedure to an operations course
